chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Abu Yahya al-Wasiti from some of our companions who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about the Magi (Zoroastrians): 'Did they have a prophet?' He said, 'Yes. Did you not receive the letter of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) to the people of Mecca: 'Embrace Islam, otherwise I will declare war against you'?' So they wrote to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family): 'Take the jizyah (tax) from us and leave us to worship our idols.' The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) wrote to them: 'I do not take the jizyah except from the People of the Book.' They wrote to him, intending to contradict him (peace be upon him and his family), saying: 'You claimed that you do not take the jizyah except from the People of the Book, yet you took the jizyah from the Magi of Hawaran.' So the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) wrote to them: 'The Magi had a prophet, whom they killed, and they burned his book. Their prophet came to them with their book in twelve thousand cowhides.'
ai.seo_question: Why did the Prophet Muhammad accept jizyah from Zoroastrians (Magi) despite saying he only takes it from People of the Book?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* provides the foundational Shia juristic argument for classifying Zoroastrians (Magi) as *Ahl al-Kitab* based on the presence of a prophet and a revealed scripture, rather than strict monotheism. It highlights the historical precedent where the Prophet Muhammad accepted *jizyah* from the Magi of Bahrain after they challenged his exclusionary stance, citing their specific prophetic lineage and twelve thousand skins of ox-hide as their holy book. This narrative underscores the flexibility in early Islamic legal practice regarding non-Muslim communities with distinct scriptural traditions.
